query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At high temperatures (500–800 °C), the overall wear resistance of thin FeNiCrCoCu coatings on steel is governed by the formation and stability of a continuous Cr₂O₃-rich tribo-oxide film at the sliding interface.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu coating (~1 µm thick) deposited on a steel substrate via PVD, tested in air at 600 °C, 10 N normal load, 5 mm/s sliding speed.
generation.intervention: Increase Cr content from 20 at% (equiatomic) to 30 at% (reducing Co accordingly) while keeping film thickness and deposition conditions unchanged.
generation.conditions: Sliding against an alumina ball in laboratory air at 600 °C ± 50 °C, normal load 10 N ± 5 N, sliding speed 5 mm/s ± 2 mm/s, steel substrate, 1 µm film thickness.
generation.structural_mediator: Thickness and continuity of the Cr₂O₃-rich tribo-oxide layer formed on the coating surface during sliding.
generation.mechanism: Higher Cr accelerates nucleation and growth of a dense Cr₂O₃ film and improves its adhesion under load, creating a continuous protective barrier that reduces direct metal–metal contact and third-body abrasion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Cr-enriched coatings will exhibit a ~30–50% lower steady-state wear rate and reduced friction coefficient, with a continuous ~100–200 nm thick Cr₂O₃ layer, compared with baseline’s discontinuous ~50 nm oxide.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu coating under identical test conditions, showing higher wear rate, higher friction, and a thinner, discontinuous oxide film.
generation.boundary: Valid for temperatures 500–800 °C, normal loads 5–20 N, sliding speeds 1–10 mm/s, film thickness ~1 µm, air environment.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of wear-rate reduction and exact oxide thickness are estimated; environmental humidity and microstructure may shift absolute values.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare equiatomic and Cr-enriched (30 at% Cr) FeNiCrCoCu coatings on steel. Conduct ball-on-flat sliding wear tests against alumina at 600 °C, 10 N, 5 mm/s in air. Characterize worn surfaces and cross sections by SEM/EDS and XPS.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-enriched coating does not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate or does not form a thicker, continuous Cr₂O₃-rich film compared to the equiatomic baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
